title: Chapter 188 – Treaty of Walls
html:
[The Garden Hall, Council Room; the Valley Wall – Lin Jian]

Jian reads the treaty three times, and each time it says something different.

The first reading is the lawyer's. He sits at the long council table in the cold gray light of a snowy morning, with Zhao on his left and a fire sputtering behind him, and goes through Han's draft clause by clause. It is a sober, careful document. Eight pages of close script, in the Sect's clerkly hand, with a red wax seal at the foot and a ribbon of cloud-blue silk. The Garden is to provide guards for sections one and two of the Wall, permanently, under the command of its own Captain. The Sect is to provide grain, twelve thousand measures at once and four thousand each winter thereafter. Pupils of the Outer Court are to spend a season each year at the Garden, learning the rhythms of the orchard. The Garden's children are to attend the Sect's lectures. A joint council will meet each equinox to settle disputes.

It is, he thinks, a good treaty. It is the sort of document that two exhausted powers write when they have discovered they cannot afford to hate each other. It is also very plainly Han's work. She has anticipated every objection. She has left no gap for pride.

The second reading is the friend's. He reads it the way he would read a letter from someone who is trying not to say what she means. Between the lines, in the choice of a word, the placement of a clause, he hears a tall stern woman bowing in the smoke. I was wrong about you. I was wrong about all of you. I do not know how to say it, so I have written eight pages.

He reads the third time for the one clause he has been avoiding.

Article Nine. The Sect of the Azure Cloud, in recognition of services rendered at the Valley Wall, offers to Lin Jian of the Garden the ancient Seat of Keeper of Walls, vacant four hundred years. The Keeper shall write his name into the arrays of the nine sections, as second key and as witness. The Keeper shall walk the Wall each dawn, as long as he is able. The Keeper shall not depart the Pass of Seven Winds, save by leave of the Seat, for the duration of his office.

He sets the paper down.

"You see the difficulty," says Zhao.

"Yes."

"Shall not depart."

"Yes."

"You have promised a child you will go to a tree." Her voice is level. She sits with her hands folded on the table, in her black mourning gown, with her white hair bound severely and her face grave. She has lost weight in a month. The lines at the corners of her mouth have deepened to grooves. "I do not say it is a reason. I say only that it is a fact. You cannot be at the Wall and at the tree."

"I could write my name and go."

"Could you?"

"The Wall does not need me present. Only named." He taps the page. "Han says so herself. In the last paragraph of her note. The name remains."

"And the oath?"

"Is a clause." He smiles faintly. "Clauses can be amended."

"Han will not like it."

"Han is a practical woman. She wants a wall. If I write my name on the arrays, the arrays will hold, whether or not I'm standing under them." He folds the treaty. "I would prefer to go and say so in person."

Zhao studies him. He sits back and lets her look. He knows what she sees: a thin white-haired man in a blanket, grayer than he was yesterday, with a cough he cannot quite suppress and eyes that have grown too large for his face. He has stopped trying to hide it. It is a strange freedom.

"You are going to accept," she says.

"I think so."

"Why?"

"Because it is the only thing left that I can do that will outlast me." He looks at his hands. "The rest of it, the Seven, the Hall, the tree, I will not see finished. I will see it begun. But a wall is a thing that stays. A name on a wall is a thing that stays." He swallows. "I would like to leave something that stays, Zhao. That's all."

She does not answer. She reaches across the table and takes his hand.

* * *

He walks out into the snow after the council, and finds that his feet have taken him to the orchard.

It is a bare place now. The black field of the tide is white with a foot of fresh powder, and the stumps stand out of it like tombstones. Here and there a new green shoot has pushed through the snow. Pia's doing, he thinks; she and the stable boys have been planting cuttings since the second week. A little way off, a gang of children is building a fort against the half-ruined wall, shrieking, hurling snowballs. Ao is among them, with his rabbit. He waves a mitten.

Jian waves back.

He goes slowly. His staff makes a small hollow sound in the snow. He passes the stump of the old pear tree, the white scar where the powder rose, and stops at the foot of the slope, where the Mother Tree stands alone against the gray sky.

It is more beautiful in winter. He had not known that. The bark is silver, the branches bare and delicate as lace, and snow lies along every limb in a thin pure line. At its foot, the ground is black. The snow will not settle there. A faint warmth rises, even now, and he can feel it on his face as he approaches. The lullaby is quieter than it was, a murmur at the edge of hearing, but it is there. He puts his hand on the trunk.

Hello, he thinks.

Nothing. Only the warmth, and the slow deep pulse.

"You are thinking about the Seat," says a voice behind him.

He turns. Yue stands in the snow, a little way off, bundled in a gray quilted cloak with a scarf wound round her head. Beside her is Mo Yan, in a boy's cloak three sizes too large, holding her hand. The small silent girl has a smear of charcoal on her cheek and a look of intense concentration. Yue's face, under the scarf, is soft and bright and slightly stunned.

"You can speak," he says.

"I've been practicing." She smiles. Her voice is cracked and odd, the voice of someone using a muscle for the first time in sixty years, but it is hers. "Mo Yan says I've an accent. She says I speak like a goat."

"A goat?"

"She drew a picture." Yue laughs, a shaky delighted laugh. "It's very rude. It was a goat in a bonnet."

He laughs too. The sound surprises him. He realizes he has not laughed properly in days.

"How long can you hold it?" he asks. "Hearing. Through her."

"An hour. Perhaps two." She glances at the child. "It costs her. I know it does. She won't say. But I see the blood. She gives me a full day of sound for a pinch of nosebleed, and she says it's fair."

"Is it?"

"I don't know." Yue's face grows serious. "I asked her tonight if I should stop. She drew a circle with a line through it. Then a bell, then a heart." She shakes her head. "I think it means no. I think it means she likes it. Is that terrible? To let a child pay for your ears?"

"I don't know," he says. "I've been paying for other people's lives with my own for some time. I'm not the one to ask."

She looks at him a long moment. Mo Yan looks at him too. The silent girl's eyes are enormous and dark, and under the grave unblinking stare he has the odd sensation of being read.

"You're going to accept the Seat," says Yue.

"How did you know?"

"Mo Yan drew it." She nods at the child. "She drew the Wall. And a man with a staff. And his hand on the stone. Then she drew a door, and the man walking through, and the Wall still standing." Yue hesitates. "I don't understand the last. But she was very certain."

Jian crouches. It takes a moment. He meets the girl's eyes, and holds out his hand, and she takes it.

"Is it right?" he says. "To accept?"

Mo Yan looks at him a long time. Then she lifts her free hand, and with her finger, in the air, she draws something. A circle. Another, inside it. A third. A tiny spiral, winding inward to a point.

It's a Core. Or a seed. Or a door.

"I don't know what that means," he says.

The girl smiles. She taps her chest, and points at him, and shrugs. I don't either.

He laughs again, helplessly, and the snow falls around them.

* * *

Bell is furious, as he knew she would be.

She finds him in the evening, in the infirmary's back room, where he has gone to sit near the stove. She comes in without knocking. She is carrying a tray with a bowl of broth and a cup of black medicine, and she sets it down on the table with a force that makes the spoon jump.

"You're taking the Seat."

"Zhao told you."

"Everyone told me. The cook told me. The dog told me." She crosses her arms. "You will go to the Pass. In the snow. With your lungs. And walk a wall for two miles every dawn, until you can't."

"I will write my name on it. I am not obliged to walk."

"I read the clause."

"It has been amended."

"I don't care if it's been amended." Her voice shakes. "I care that you're going to spend the last eleven weeks of your life in a place where I can't reach you."

He looks at her. She stands rigid, white-lipped, with her arms folded tight across her chest like a woman holding in a scream. Her hair is coming out of its tie. There is flour on her sleeve, and a smear of green on her cheek, and her eyes are red.

"Bell," he says gently. "Sit down."

"No."

"Then stand. But listen." He sets the cup aside. "I did not ask for the Seat. It was offered. I will take it for one reason. It gives me a way to stay useful without being in the room. The Wall will carry my name. The Sect will have its keystones. And I will be free to do the one thing that matters, which is get to the tree." He takes a breath. "I will not be at the Wall. I will be here. I will be where you can reach me."

"Until the tree."

"Until the tree."

"And after?"

He is silent.

Bell turns away. She walks to the small window, and stands with her back to him, looking out at the dark. A long time passes. The stove ticks. When she speaks, her voice is steady, and very small.

"I'm a healer," she says. "That's all I've ever been. When my mother died, I thought, I will learn how to stop it. When my sister died, I thought, I will learn faster. I have been learning faster for twenty years." She laughs, a short dry sound. "And here you are. And I have nothing. Not a drop. Not a leaf. Nothing in my books that will give you one day more."

"You've given me nine weeks of good coughing."

"Don't joke."

"I'm not." He rises. It takes him two tries. He crosses the room and stands beside her, not touching. "You told me to make them good months. You told me. I have been doing it. It has been the best month of my life, Bell. I've eaten Qinghe's soup and listened to Feng's drums and watched a boy named Tao fall off a wall. I have been happy. Do you understand? I have been happier these four weeks than in the previous forty years. You did that."

She says nothing. Her shoulders shake.

"So stop looking for a leaf," he says. "You already found it."

She turns and puts her forehead against his chest, hard, and stays there. He puts his arms around her. They stand that way a long time in the small warm room, with the stove ticking and the snow falling past the window, and neither of them says a word.

* * *

He visits Wenyuan last, in the dead of night, when there is nobody to see.

The winter room is at the top of the Hall, under the eaves, a long low chamber with a slanted ceiling and a single window. A banked fire glows in the grate. In the center, on a low bed, under three quilts, his father lies asleep. He has not moved since the first frost. His face is smooth and young, a face of forty, and his hands are folded on his chest. The breath that stirs the quilt is shallow and slow.

Jian sits on the stool beside the bed. He rests the staff against the wall.

"Father," he says.

The old man sleeps.

"I have a thing to tell you. Several, actually. I don't suppose you can hear." He rubs his face with his hands. "Qinghe formed a Core. She'll tell you. She's very proud, and she'll pretend she isn't. Yue speaks. You'll want to hear it. It's rather like a goat, but she's delighted. Tian Mo has a new arm. Lan Wen is dead." His voice cracks. "Pei An. Dao. Gu, whom you never met. A great many others."

The fire pops.

"I'm signing the Seat tomorrow. It will keep a wall standing. It's a small thing. I thought you would want to know."

He is quiet for a time.

"I'm sorry I won't be here when you wake," he says at last. "I was looking forward to it. I had a speech prepared." A wan smile. "It was terrible. I'll spare you."

Then he lifts his father's hand from the quilt, a cool dry hand, with the old callus on the palm from a hundred years of hoeing, and holds it between both of his. He thinks of a small boy holding it in the dark, on a night that smelled of wood smoke and wet earth, and a deep quiet voice saying there's nothing in the dark that wasn't in the light.

"I think you were right," he says. "I think I was only afraid of the wrong things."

He sits there until the fire burns low. Then he lays the hand back on the quilt, and tucks it in, takes up his staff, and goes down the stairs.

* * *

They sign on the ninth section of the Wall, in a high wind, on the thirtieth day after the tide.

It is not a grand ceremony. Han has forbidden pomp. A table is carried out onto the parapet, and a lamp, and a brazier for the wax. There are only a handful of witnesses: Zhao in her black gown with Qinghe at her side; Lu Fei with his Weights; Sera, stiff in her Captain's cloak; a dozen of the Elders, huddled against the wind in their gray robes. Elder Mu is not among them. His chair, Jian is told, is empty.

Han stands at the head of the table. She has put on her formal robe, the dark blue silk with the cloud-sigil on the breast, and she wears it as a woman wears armor. Her face is calm. Her eyes, when they meet his, are not.

"Elder Lin," she says.

"Head Han."

"You have read the draft."

"I have."

"Do you wish to amend it?"

"One clause." He steps forward. "Article Nine."

"I thought you might."

"The oath of residence. The Keeper shall not depart the Pass." He keeps his voice even. "I will accept the Seat. I will write my name into the arrays, all nine, in my own hand. But I cannot swear never to leave. I have a promise to keep elsewhere. It is made to a child, and it is the last thing I mean to do."

A silence. The wind snaps the banners.

Han looks at him for a long time. Then, slowly, she nods.

"Lu Fei," she says.

"Head?"

"Strike the clause."

"Head, the Founders' charter specifically..."

"The Founders' charter specifies a Keeper who can walk the Wall. It says nothing about one who cannot. I am the Head of this Sect. I shall interpret." She turns back to Jian. "Elder. I offered you a Seat. I did not offer you a cage. If I have written one by accident, I beg your pardon."

"You wrote it out of habit."

"That is not an excuse."

"No." He smiles. "But I forgive it."

She almost smiles back. She turns to the table, picks up a pen, and with a short firm stroke crosses through the last paragraph of Article Nine. She initials it. She hands him the brush.

He hesitates.

It is a small thing, a brush of dark horsehair with a bone handle, worn smooth by long use. The ink in the stone beside it is thick and black. The page lies before him, spread under the lamp, with a line left blank at the foot for his name. He looks at it. He thinks, for no reason, of Qinghe's spoon, and Wenyuan's quilt, and the sound of Feng's drums, and the girl with a dimple and a grass stain on her knee.

Make them good months.

He dips the brush. He writes.

The characters come slowly. His hand shakes. But the strokes are firm, black, even, and when he lifts the brush from the paper, the name is there, plain as a seal: Lin Jian.

Nothing happens.

Then the Wall begins to hum.

* * *

It starts in the stone beneath his feet, a low deep note that rises through his bones, and spreads along the parapet like fire along a fuse. The lamp flares. The ink on the page glows a pale gold. And from the ninth buttress, from the plaque with Gu's name, a thread of light runs out across the stone, thin and bright, and reaches for the paper.

It touches his signature.

The name lifts. It rises off the page in a ribbon of golden script, turns once in the air like a leaf, and flows down into the stone of the Wall. He watches it go. It runs along the parapet in both directions, eight sections, nine, and as it goes the markers flicker alive, one by one, and the Weights on their cords begin to swing. At section three the light steadies. At section five it surges. By the time it reaches the far end, a mile away, the whole Wall is shining softly in the gray dawn, a long gold line against the snow.

"By the Founders," whispers Lu Fei.

The pupils on the parapet are staring. A murmur runs along the line, and then a sound that Jian does not at first recognize. It is a cheer. Not loud. A low, hoarse, astonished breath, spreading from throat to throat.

Beside him Han has put her hand to her mouth.

"It took," she says, in an odd voice. "It took the first time."

"Is that unusual?"

"The record says it took Gu nine days." She shakes her head. "Nine days, and a hundred pupils, and the lives of three Elders. You wrote one name."

"I had help," he says.

He turns his head. Behind him, in the shadow of the buttress, a thin pale light is fading from the stone. For a moment he thought he saw a face in it, small and grave and silver, with a dimple in the left cheek. He cannot be sure. It may have been the wind.

Thank you, he thinks, to nobody.

You're welcome, says nobody, very faintly, in a voice like a bell.

* * *

He does not mean to scan the page.

It is habit, only. A thing his mind reaches for, the way a man reaches for his belt-knife in the dark. They have signed; Han has put the seal to it; the Elders are clapping each other on the shoulder, and Zhao and Qinghe are talking quietly at the end of the table. He stands apart, a little dizzy, looking at the signed treaty lying open in the lamplight. His own name, in black. Han's, in blue. Zhao's, in red. And at the foot of the page, stamped into the wax in a deep clean impression, the Sect's cloud-sigil.

He has seen it a hundred times.

But he has never looked at it. Not as an object. Not as a thing with a shape. Tonight, for some reason, the pattern catches at his eye: a spiral of three curved lines, winding inward to a point, with a tiny cross at the center. It is a Sect seal. It is on every banner and every robe. It is on the plaque of the ninth buttress. It is the first thing he saw when he walked into the Outer Court, a boy of thirteen, nine decades ago.

A circle. Another, inside it. A third. A tiny spiral, winding inward to a point.

He goes cold.

Mo Yan, he thinks. You drew it in the snow.

He lifts his hand. He knows what it costs. He has been spending days like small coins, and he has perhaps seventy left, and one of them is about to go. He does it anyway.

Scan.

Type: Seal (wax, ceremonial) -- Azure Cloud Sect
Pattern: triple spiral with central cross
Origin: Gate sigil, class V (non-public)
Match: 100% -- Lead terminus mark, Gate lead (monofilament)
Associated operator: THE VEILED (Nine, seat 4)
Note: Sect founding charter, year 1, authenticated with this mark.

He reads it. He reads it again.

The Veiled.

He remembers the vision in the Alpha's chamber. A tall figure, veiled and hooded, bending over the young Moonhorn with a silver rod. One of the Nine. One of the vow-makers. A woman who drove a wire into a living creature and called it necessary. And on the page before him, in the red wax of the Sect's oldest seal, the same sigil.

The Sect's founding charter, authenticated with this mark.

He raises his head. Han is across the table, speaking to Lu Fei, her tall figure silhouetted against the pale sky. Beyond her the Wall stretches away into the dawn, shining, gold, humming with his name. A line of banners hangs limp in the cold. On each of them, stitched in white silk, is the triple spiral.

The Sect did not build the Wall, he thinks. The Sect was built to keep it.

Who was the Veiled? And what did they hide in the Pass?

"Elder?" says Han. She has turned. She is looking at him across the table with a faint quizzical frown. "You look unwell."

"I'm well."

"You've gone gray."

"I have been gray for a month." He tries to smile and cannot quite manage it. "Head Han. A question. The Sect's seal. The triple spiral. Do you know where it came from?"

"The Founders." She shrugs. "It is the oldest mark we have. The first Head chose it. They say she was a veiled woman who never showed her face. The scholars have argued for centuries about what it means."

"A veiled woman."

"A legend, I should think. Why?"

He opens his mouth. Closes it.

The wind plucks at the treaty. The wax gleams red under the lamp. And on the stone beneath his feet, very faintly, he can feel his own name running through the Wall like a pulse, humming, eager, bound.

Eight weeks, he thinks. Perhaps ten. To find out who built the thing I have just promised to keep.

"No reason," he says. "I was only curious."

Han studies him a moment longer. Then she nods, and turns back, and he stands in the wind with the signed treaty before him and a question in his chest like a stone.
